content:
Anthropic’s new default model on Claude Max arrived on July 24 with examples of a model that verifies and retries. An outside benchmark published the same day is less impressed.

5 min read
Just now

--

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Anthropic’s launch artwork for Claude Opus 5, released on July 24. Image: Anthropic.Anthropic gave Claude Opus 5 a drawing of a machine part and asked it to write code that would rebuild the part as a 3D model in FreeCAD. The test deliberately withheld any way for the model to view that drawing. Rather than stop there, Opus 5 wrote its own computer vision code, worked out the geometry of the part from what that code returned, and reconstructed it. Anthropic says it managed this repeatedly, and that no competing model given the same setup solved the task after five attempts.
That example is the company’s own, taken from a benchmark it built and published in the post announcing Claude Opus 5 on July 24. It is also the clearest statement of what Anthropic says separates this release from Opus 4.8, which is the model checking its own work and retrying when the first approach fails.
Where it stands on the day of release:

• Default model on Claude Max, and the most capable option available to Claude Pro subscribers

• $5 and $25 per million input and output tokens through the API, the same list price as Opus 4.8

• Also running on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud and Microsoft Foundry

• Released 45 days after Fable 5 and Mythos 5, which arrived on June 9
What it does that Opus 4.8 did not
Anthropic’s examples are variations on a single behaviour, which is checking the work instead of accepting the first thing that looks right:

• A bug in an open-source package manager. Opus 5 traced the root cause and fixed an edge case that the community’s own patch had missed. A competing model patched the visible symptom and reported the bug resolved.

• A market data feed at a trading firm. An engineer built it for a new exchange in a single session, and with no live feed available to validate against, the model wrote its own test harness to check it was parsing the exchange’s data correctly. Anthropic says previous models could not complete the task at all.

• A retention workflow at Zapier. Wade Foster reports that the model took a raw account-health workbook and ran a full churn-prevention sequence end to end, flagging at-risk accounts, alerting the right owner and summarising for the retention team, where earlier models had not passed at all.

• A design argument. Marquis Wang, a principal AI engineer, proposed a design during a rearchitecting session. The model disagreed, held its position when he insisted, narrowed the objection to a single design question and offered a compromise that kept the part of his idea that worked.
The benchmark numbers point the same way. On Zapier’s AutomationBench the pass rate is around 1.5 times the next best model at the same cost per task. On Frontier-Bench v0.1 Opus 5 more than doubles Opus 4.8’s score while costing less per task, and on CursorBench 3.2 at maximum effort it lands within 0.5% of Fable 5, a model that sells at twice the price. A legal AI team reports quality comparable to Opus 4.8 while generating 26% fewer tokens at maximum reasoning.
All of these accounts come from Anthropic’s launch post, and the named ones come from customers with a commercial relationship with the company.
What an outside test found
CodeRabbit published its own benchmark the same day, testing code review rather than code generation, and the result cuts both ways. At x-high effort Opus 5 produced the cleanest stream of actionable comments they have measured, 39.3% precision against a 35.2% baseline, but it caught fewer of the benchmark’s known issues, 55.2% against 61.1%, generated roughly four times as many nitpicks, and saw its precision across the full post-pipeline stream fall below baseline, 28.6% against 32.8%. Their verdict is that Opus 5 is not the best general-purpose reviewer they have tested, and that it fits as a second precision-oriented lane rather than as the only reviewer or the safety net on high-risk changes. One of their engineers described it as less anxious than earlier Opus models.
Their most useful finding concerns the effort setting. Raising the reasoning level changed what the model traded off instead of making the review better, so they advise testing the low and medium settings rather than assuming that more effort produces a better result.
Three things with an asterisk
Requests flagged by Anthropic’s safety classifiers now fall back to Opus 4.8 by default inside Claude.ai, Claude Code and Claude Cowork, so an answer occasionally arrives from a model other than the one selected.
On safety, Anthropic’s automated audit rates Opus 5 as its least misaligned model to date and says it follows Claude’s Constitution more closely than Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5 or Fable 5. On cybersecurity it stays behind Mythos 5, particularly at turning a vulnerability into a working exploit.
During the two weeks the model circulated inside Cursor before launch under the codename Honeycomb EAP, developer @chetaslua reported it consuming tokens faster than Fable 5 and using up his quota in three prompts. For subscribers the effect of that would show up as hitting the usage limit sooner.
One first-hand note, covering a few hours of use rather than anything measured. The behaviour I noticed first is that Opus 5 does not fold. Asking earlier models to reconsider an answer usually produced agreement within a turn or two, whatever the merits of the objection. This one holds its position, names the part of the objection it accepts, and asks what specifically I think is wrong before changing anything. That lines up with the design argument in the list above, which is the one item in Anthropic’s launch material describing a behaviour rather than a score.

Marc Bara is a project management consultant and educator with a PhD in Electrical Engineering. He writes about AI, work, and project management. Find him on LinkedIn.
